title: When courts are too slow, police replace judges
syllabus: GS2 › Structure, organisation and functioning of the judiciary; Police reforms · GS4 › Probity in governance
context: Abhinav Chandrachud argues that years-long civil suits push well-connected litigants to the police, who turn debt and contract disputes into criminal cases of 'cheating' or 'breach of trust'. This creates a parallel, coercive civil-justice system.
ideas: Delay breeds a 'parallel justice' system: police summons and threats of arrest replace a court's verdict.
Judicial delay has bred 'parallel justice', with police summons and arrest threats replacing a court's verdict in civil disputes.
The root is too few judges: about 15 per million people in Maharashtra against about 157 in New York state.
Maharashtra has about 15 judges per million people against about 157 in New York state; vacancies feed delay.
Using criminal law to settle a civil debt is abuse of process; the Supreme Court has discouraged it, but practice lags the law.
GS2 rule of law · GS4 probity
Turning a civil debt into a criminal case is abuse of process, discouraged by the Supreme Court but common in practice.
keywords: Turning debt or contract quarrels into 'cheating' cases
